sources.name: Shapur I's inscription on the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht (ŠKZ)

works.note: On the 'Cube of Zoroaster' at Naqsh-e Rustam: Shapur's three Roman wars: Gordian III killed at Misiche (244) and Philip paying 500,000 denarii; destruction of a Roman army of 60,000 at Barbalissos (253) and the sack of 37 cities including Antioch; the capture of Valerian 'with our own hands' near Carrhae and Edessa (260), with lists of captured praetorian prefect, senators and the deportation of Romans into Iran.

sources.reliability: The Persian counter-narrative to Roman sources for the 240s-260s; its battle claims (Misiche) conflict with Roman accounts of Gordian's death. Also lists the provinces of the empire and the fire temples endowed.
sources.summary: Royal inscription of Shapur I, c. 262; companion to the rock reliefs of Naqsh-e Rustam and Bishapur showing Valerian kneeling.

sources.name: Antonine Itinerary

works.note: 225 routes with stations and distances in miles (leagues in Gaul); core probably compiled under Caracalla, revised under Diocletian.

sources.reliability: Register of road routes across the empire, the backbone for locating Roman road stations (including 15 British routes). Not a map; distances are corrupted in places.
sources.summary: Compiled from cursus publicus records.

sources.name: Tabula Peutingeriana

works.books: 11 surviving parchment segments, 6.75 m long; the westernmost (Britain, Spain) lost
works.note: 13th-century copy of a late antique road map, now in Vienna. Date of the original disputed (c. 300 Talbert; c. 435 Weber; with Augustan or earlier strata).

sources.reliability: Schematic diagram of the road network from Britain to India with hundreds of settlement symbols and some 3,000 named features, stretched east-west; Constantinople, Rome and Antioch shown as personifications.
sources.summary: Named after Konrad Peutinger, the Augsburg humanist who owned it.

sources.name: Panegyrici Latini

works.books: 12 speeches: Pliny's Panegyricus plus 11 Gallic speeches of 289-389
works.note: To Maximian (289, 291), Constantius (297, on the recovery of Britain), Constantine (307, 310 with the vision of Apollo, 311, 313, 321), Julian (Mamertinus, 362) and Theodosius (Pacatus, 389).

sources.reliability: Court rhetoric, but contemporary and often the only source for Tetrarchic campaigns and Constantine's shifting self-presentation (the Claudius Gothicus ancestry first appears in 310).
sources.summary: Collected at Autun/Trier rhetorical circles.

sources.name: Edict on Maximum Prices

works.books: Preamble and 32 sections, c. 1,200 items, reconstructed from over 40 fragmentary copies, almost all in the Greek east (Aphrodisias the longest)
works.note: Issued late 301 (after 20 Nov) in the names of the Tetrarchs; prices in denarii communes for grain, wine, meat, textiles, wages (farm labourer 25 denarii a day with food), freight by sea and land.

sources.reliability: Unique source for relative prices and transport costs (land carriage of wheat for 300 miles roughly doubled its price; sea transport far cheaper). The preamble blames avarice; Lactantius says it caused shortages and bloodshed and was abandoned.
sources.summary: Diocletianic legislation accompanying the currency revaluation edict of Sep 301.

sources.name: Verona List

works.note: Seventh-century manuscript list of the 12 dioceses and about 100 provinces, dated c. 314 (Barnes; Jones c. 312-320), with a list of barbarian peoples.

sources.reliability: Primary evidence for Diocletian's subdivision of provinces and the creation of dioceses; some entries reflect later revisions.
sources.summary: Preserved in a Verona chapter library manuscript.

sources.name: Lactantius

works.note: Death of persecutors from Nero to Maximinus Daza, detailed for 303-313: the Great Persecution, Diocletian's abdication, Constantine's dream before the Milvian Bridge (the chi-rho shield sign), and the text of the 'edict of Milan' (Licinius' letter of 313).

sources.reliability: Hostile to Diocletian and Galerius, but a contemporary in Nicomedia; preserves the texts of Galerius' edict of toleration (311) and the 313 rescript. His account of Diocletian's 'four rulers' and tax burdens is caricature with a factual core.
sources.summary: North African rhetor appointed by Diocletian at Nicomedia, later tutor of Constantine's son Crispus at Trier.

sources.name: Eusebius of Caesarea

works.books: 10 books, several editions (to c. 313 and c. 325)
works.note: Quotes documents verbatim, including imperial rescripts to Christians.
Constantine's oath-sworn account of the vision of the cross; imperial letters quoted.
Synchronized tables from Abraham to 325; survives in Jerome's Latin version and an Armenian translation.

sources.reliability: Founder of church history and Christian chronography; invaluable documents, but a panegyrist of Constantine who suppresses unwelcome facts (Crispus' execution).
sources.summary: Bishop of Caesarea Maritima from c. 313; at Nicaea (325).

sources.name: Anonymus Valesianus

works.note: Concise, factual account of Constantine's career, probably c. 340-390.
Odoacer and Theodoric, with the end of Boethius and Symmachus; mid-6th century, Ravenna perspective.

sources.reliability: Two unrelated texts named after their editor Henri de Valois (1636); both reliable and terse.
sources.summary: Anonymous.

sources.name: Chronograph of 354

works.note: Illustrated calendar compiled by Furius Dionysius Filocalus: consular fasti from 509 BC, Easter tables, city prefects 254-354, Depositio episcoporum and Depositio martyrum (first record of 25 Dec as Christ's birth), list of bishops of Rome, regionary catalogue of the city, Chronica urbis Romae.

sources.reliability: Survives in Renaissance copies of a lost Carolingian manuscript; key for late antique Rome's calendar and administration.
sources.summary: Commissioned by the Christian aristocrat Valentinus.

sources.name: Aurelius Victor

works.note: Written 361; Augustus to Constantius II, moralizing on the decline of senatorial standards and the army.

sources.reliability: Short imperial history from the lost Kaisergeschichte (Enmann's hypothesis) with independent interpretive views; valuable for the 3rd century.
sources.summary: African of humble origin; governor of Pannonia Secunda under Julian (361), prefect of Rome 389.

sources.name: Epitome de Caesaribus

works.note: Augustus to the death of Theodosius I; distinct from Victor and with independent information (e.g. on Constantine's birth, Theodosius).

sources.reliability: Anonymous, wrongly ascribed to Victor in manuscripts; uses the Kaisergeschichte, Marius Maximus and other lost sources.
sources.summary: Written soon after 395.

sources.name: Eutropius

works.note: Dedicated to Valens (369/370); translated into Greek by Paeanius and much used in Byzantium.

sources.reliability: Clear, neutral summary based on Livy's epitome, Suetonius and the Kaisergeschichte; reliable in outline, especially for the 3rd-4th centuries. An eyewitness of Julian's Persian campaign.
sources.summary: Magister memoriae under Valens; proconsul of Asia, praetorian prefect of Illyricum (380-381), consul 387.

sources.name: Festus

works.note: Short survey of the acquisition of provinces and the wars with Persia, written c. 370 for Valens' eastern campaign.

sources.reliability: Valuable for the provincial list and the sequence of Roman-Persian wars; otherwise thin.
sources.summary: Magister memoriae of Valens.

sources.name: Julian (writings)

works.t: Orations, letters, Caesars, Misopogon, Letter to the Athenians
works.note: The Letter to the Athenians (361) justifies his usurpation; Misopogon (363) satirizes Antioch; c. 80 letters, including religious edicts (the school law of 362).

sources.reliability: An emperor's own voice, unusual for antiquity; partisan but revealing on his pagan restoration and campaigns.

sources.name: Libanius

works.note: Funeral oration for Julian (Or. 18), On the temples (Or. 30), on patronage of villages (Or. 47), on the riots of 387 (Or. 19-23).

sources.reliability: The largest letter collection of antiquity; a pagan rhetor's view of urban life, curial decline and imperial officials in 4th-century Antioch.
sources.summary: Sophist at Antioch; teacher of John Chrysostom (by tradition).

sources.name: Ammianus Marcellinus

works.note: Gallus Caesar, Silvanus, the siege of Amida (359, which he escaped), Julian's Gallic and Persian campaigns, Valentinian and Valens, the Huns and Adrianople.

sources.reliability: The last great Latin historian and the best source for any late Roman period: an officer (protector domesticus) who served under Ursicinus and Julian. Fair-minded pagan, but with hostility to Valentinian's regime and satirical excursuses on Rome's aristocracy.
sources.summary: Greek from Antioch writing in Latin at Rome c. 390.

sources.name: Eunapius

works.note: Main source of Zosimus for 270-404.

sources.reliability: Hostile to Christians and Theodosius; Photius found him verbose. Known mainly through Zosimus and the Constantinian excerpts.
sources.summary: Sophist of Sardis.

sources.name: Jerome

works.note: Translation of Eusebius' canons with additions on Roman history and a continuation 325-378.
Letter 123 on the barbarian invasions of Gaul (406-409); Letter 127 on the sack of Rome.

sources.reliability: Annalistic notices on the 4th century (often from the Kaisergeschichte); letters give vivid if rhetorical reactions to 410.
sources.summary: Biblical translator (the Vulgate), at Bethlehem from 386.

sources.name: Symmachus

works.books: 49 official reports as prefect of Rome
works.note: Relatio 3 (384) pleads for the restoration of the Altar of Victory: 'uno itinere non potest perveniri ad tam grande secretum'.

sources.reliability: Window on the pagan senatorial elite and the administration of Rome (grain supply, games).
sources.summary: Prefect of Rome 384-385, consul 391.

sources.name: Claudian

works.note: Panegyrics on the consulships of Honorius and Stilicho; invectives against Rufinus and Eutropius; De bello Gildonico, De bello Getico (Pollentia, 402).

sources.reliability: Stilicho's court poet: the only near-contemporary western narrative for 395-404, heavily slanted.
sources.summary: Alexandrian Greek writing Latin at Milan and Ravenna.

sources.name: Vegetius

works.note: Recruitment, training, legion organization, siegecraft, naval warfare; dedicated to an emperor (Theodosius I or Valentinian III).

sources.reliability: Antiquarian idealization of the 'ancient legion' drawn from Cato, Celsus, Frontinus and Paternus, set against the decline of his own day; reliability on contemporary practice disputed.
sources.summary: Senior civil official (vir illustris, comes).

sources.name: Notitia Dignitatum
sources.latin: Notitia dignitatum omnium tam civilium quam militarium

works.note: Eastern part c. 395-401; western part revised piecemeal to c. 420s. Lists every high office, its staff (officium), insignia, and the several hundred military units under each commander, with illustrations of shield emblems and fortifications.

sources.reliability: The fundamental document for the late Roman state and army. A paper picture: some units and offices may have existed only nominally, and the western list mixes dates.
sources.summary: Copies from a lost Carolingian manuscript (Codex Spirensis).

sources.name: Codex Theodosianus

works.books: 16 books, over 2,500 constitutions from 312 to 437; books 1-5 incomplete
works.note: Promulgated 15 Feb 438, in force in the West from 1 Jan 439; book 16 on religion (heresy, Jews, pagan cults). With the Sirmondian Constitutions and post-Theodosian Novels.

sources.reliability: Laws excerpted and dated; the repetition of laws shows enforcement problems rather than mere legislative activity. Indispensable for the coloni, curiales, army and church.
sources.summary: Compiled by a commission under Theodosius II (429-438).

sources.name: Orosius

works.note: From Ninus to 417; book 7 has unique material on 400-417 (Radagaisus, Athaulf's wish to restore Rome with Gothic strength).

sources.reliability: Written at Augustine's request to show disasters were worse before Christ; poor on the distant past (from Livy and Eutropius), useful for the contemporary West.
sources.summary: Priest from Bracara (Braga) who fled the Vandals to Africa.

sources.name: Olympiodorus of Thebes

works.note: Summarized by Photius; used by Zosimus 5-6 and Sozomen.

sources.reliability: Diplomat whose memoir is the best source for the West 407-425 (Constantine III, Athaulf and Placidia, Constantius III); records Roman senatorial incomes (up to 4,000 lb of gold a year).
sources.summary: Egyptian poet-diplomat; embassy to the Huns c. 412.

sources.name: Philostorgius

works.note: Arian (Eunomian) perspective; secular material on Stilicho, the Goths and the Huns.

sources.reliability: The only heterodox church history to survive in any form; useful for secular events and Arian bishops.
sources.summary: Cappadocian layman.

sources.name: Socrates Scholasticus
sources.reliability: Careful, moderate lawyer-historian continuing Eusebius; corrected his first edition after reading Athanasius. Records Hypatia's murder (415) and secular events in Constantinople.
sources.summary: Lay advocate in Constantinople.

sources.name: Sozomen

works.books: 9 books; planned to 439 but ends c. 425
works.note: Draws on Socrates and Olympiodorus; information on Persian Christians, monasticism and the West.

sources.reliability: Literary rewriting of Socrates with additions; dedicated to Theodosius II.
sources.summary: Lawyer from near Gaza.

sources.name: Theodoret of Cyrrhus

works.note: Includes the penance of Theodosius after Thessalonica (390).

sources.reliability: Strongly anti-Arian; preserves letters and creeds. His Religious History of Syrian monks is also historical evidence.
sources.summary: Bishop of Cyrrhus, a theologian of the Antiochene school.

sources.name: Zosimus

works.books: 6 books, the last unfinished (breaks off just before the sack of Rome, 410)
works.note: Book 1 sketches Augustus to 270 briefly, then the 3rd century from Dexippus; a lacuna removes 282-305; books 2-5 use Eunapius, 5-6 Olympiodorus.

sources.reliability: Pagan answer to Orosius: Rome declined because the old gods were abandoned (blames Constantine). Quality mirrors his sources; careless with geography and names.
sources.summary: Comes and advocatus fisci in Constantinople, writing c. 498-518.

sources.name: Hydatius

works.note: Continues Jerome; eyewitness of the Suevic kingdom in Gallaecia, Visigothic campaigns in Spain and embassies to Aetius (431).

sources.reliability: Apocalyptic in tone (expecting the end in 482), chronology sometimes faulty, but unique for 5th-century Spain.
sources.summary: Bishop of Aquae Flaviae (Chaves) in Gallaecia.

sources.name: Prosper of Aquitaine

works.note: Continues Jerome from 379; own material for 425-455 including Aetius, Attila in Italy (452) and Pope Leo.

sources.reliability: Terse but contemporary in Rome for the age of Aetius; Augustinian theologian.
sources.summary: Secretary to Pope Leo I.

sources.name: Priscus

works.books: 8 books; substantial fragments in the Constantinian Excerpta de legationibus
works.note: Contains his eyewitness account of the embassy to Attila (449): Attila's wooden palace, his simple wooden cup, the Greek merchant turned Hun who praised life under Attila.

sources.reliability: Thucydidean-style history of high quality; the main source for the Huns and eastern diplomacy; Jordanes' Attila chapters derive from him.
sources.summary: Rhetor from Panium in Thrace, on Maximinus' embassy of 449.

sources.name: Malchus

works.note: Zeno's reign, Theodoric Strabo and Theodoric the Amal, the embassy of Odoacer's senate returning the western regalia.

sources.reliability: Fragments of high quality via the Constantinian excerpts and Photius.
sources.summary: Sophist from Philadelphia (Amman).

sources.name: Sidonius Apollinaris

works.books: 9 books of 147 letters; 24 poems including panegyrics on Avitus (456), Majorian (458) and Anthemius (468)
works.note: Portrait of Theodoric II (Ep. 1.2); the defence of Clermont against Euric (471-475).

sources.reliability: The fullest picture of the Gallo-Roman elite as the western empire dissolved, in a precious style.
sources.summary: Son-in-law of Avitus; prefect of Rome 468; bishop of Clermont from c. 470.

sources.name: Victor of Vita

works.note: Includes Huneric's edict of 484 and the list of exiled bishops (Notitia provinciarum et civitatum Africae).

sources.reliability: Catholic polemic against the Vandal Arian kings; exaggerates but preserves documents and the 484 bishop list.
sources.summary: African cleric, probably bishop.

sources.name: Laterculus of Polemius Silvius

works.note: List of the provinces of the empire by diocese appended to a calendar dedicated to Bishop Eucherius of Lyon, plus lists of emperors, animals and Roman buildings.

sources.reliability: A mid-5th-century provincial list from Gaul that mixes current and outdated information; compared with the Verona List and Notitia for provincial change.
sources.summary: Compiled by Polemius Silvius in Gaul, 448/449.

sources.name: Chronicle of Pseudo-Joshua the Stylite

works.note: Edessa during the Anastasian war with Kavad I (502-506): famine, plague, prices, the sieges of Amida and Edessa.

sources.reliability: A remarkably precise local chronicle with grain prices and military detail; preserved within the Chronicle of Zuqnin.
sources.summary: Anonymous Edessene monk (not Joshua), written c. 507.

sources.name: Marcellinus Comes

works.note: Eastern perspective; continuation to 548 by another hand. Notes under 476: 'the western empire of the Roman people... perished with this Augustulus'.

sources.reliability: Official-minded chronicle; first source to treat 476 as the end of the western empire.
sources.summary: Illyrian, cancellarius of Justinian.

sources.name: Cassiodorus

works.note: Letters drafted for Theodoric, Athalaric, Amalasuntha, Theodahad and Witiges, and in his own name as praetorian prefect.
Consular list with notes to 519.
Lost; used by Jordanes.

sources.reliability: Primary documents of Ostrogothic government, cast in elaborate rhetoric; Romano-Gothic accommodation ideology.
sources.summary: Senator, quaestor, magister officiorum and praetorian prefect; founded the monastery of Vivarium.

sources.name: Jordanes

works.note: Gothic history from Scandza to 551; Catalaunian Plains from Priscus; earlier parts legendary (Goths conflated with Getae and Scythians).
Compilation from Florus, Eutropius, Jerome and Marcellinus, with original notes for the 6th-century Balkans.

sources.reliability: Abridges Cassiodorus' lost Gothic history (from memory, he says); a pro-Justinian Goth. Unique for some 5th-century events, but ethnogenesis passages are literary constructions.
sources.summary: Of Gothic-Alan descent, notarius of a magister militum, later a cleric in Constantinople.

sources.name: Procopius

works.books: 8 books: Persian (1-2, to 549), Vandalic (3-4, background from 395; to 548), Gothic (5-7, 535-551), book 8 (to 553/554)
works.note: Eyewitness as Belisarius' assessor 527-540: Dara, the Nika riot, Ad Decimum, the siege of Rome; the plague of 542 at Constantinople (2.22-23).
Written c. 550, unpublished in his lifetime: savage invective on Justinian and Theodora, Belisarius and Antonina.
Panegyric of Justinian's building programme: Hagia Sophia, Danube forts, Dara.

sources.reliability: The best historian of late antiquity and the main source for Justinian's wars; classicizing (Thucydides, Herodotus), so Christian and administrative matters are muted. The three works pull in different directions, reflecting a politically constrained author.
sources.summary: From Caesarea in Palestine; lawyer and legal assessor to Belisarius.

sources.name: Corpus Juris Civilis

works.books: 12 books, c. 4,600 constitutions from Hadrian to 534
works.note: First edition 529 (lost); second 534.

works.books: 50 books, excerpts from 39 classical jurists (Ulpian about a third, Paul a sixth), promulgated 16 Dec 533
works.note: Classical law of the 1st century BC to the 230s, edited (interpolated) by Tribonian's commission.

works.books: c. 168 new laws, mostly in Greek
works.note: Administrative reforms, e.g. Novel 8 against sale of offices, the provincial reorganizations of 535-536.

sources.reliability: The codification of Roman law; the Digest is the main source for classical jurisprudence, though interpolations must be detected; the Code shows imperial rescripts in action.
sources.summary: Compiled under Justinian by commissions led by Tribonian (528-534).

sources.name: John the Lydian

works.note: History of Roman offices from the kings, focused on the decline of the praetorian prefecture under John the Cappadocian; gives Diocletian's army figures.

sources.reliability: Embittered bureaucrat's insider view of the eastern civil service; antiquarian errors about early Rome, real knowledge of 6th-century administration.
sources.summary: Official in the praetorian prefecture 511-551, professor of Latin at Constantinople.

sources.name: Gildas

works.note: The appeal to Aetius 'thrice consul' (446-454), the invitation to the Saxons by a 'proud tyrant', Ambrosius Aurelianus, Mons Badonicus.

sources.reliability: A sermon, not a history: chronology confused and Roman Britain misunderstood, but the only near-contemporary British narrative of the 5th-6th centuries.
sources.summary: British monk, writing c. 530-545.

sources.name: Corippus

works.note: John Troglita's campaigns against the Moors.
Justin II's accession and ceremonial.

sources.reliability: Epic panegyric giving unique detail on Moorish tribes and Byzantine Africa, and on court ceremonial.
sources.summary: African grammarian.

sources.name: John Malalas

works.books: 18 books; the main manuscript breaks off in 563
works.note: World chronicle from Adam; Antioch-centred, rich for 5th-6th century earthquakes, riots, circus factions, the Nika revolt and Justinian's laws.

sources.reliability: Naïve and error-prone on early history, but contemporary for c. 500-565 and an important source for urban life and the eastern frontier; the first Byzantine popular chronicle.
sources.summary: Syrian rhetor ('malal' = orator) from Antioch, later in Constantinople.

sources.name: Agathias

works.note: Narses in Italy (Casilinum 554), war in Lazica, the Kutrigur raid of 559 repulsed by the aged Belisarius; excursus on Sasanian kings from the Persian royal annals, obtained via the interpreter Sergius.

sources.reliability: Continuator of Procopius; more moralizing, weaker on military detail, but his Persian chapters use genuine Sasanian records. Source of the army figure of 150,000 under Justinian.
sources.summary: Lawyer and poet from Myrina.

sources.name: Evagrius Scholasticus

works.note: From the Council of Ephesus to 594; personal account of the plague of 542 and its recurrences, which killed his wife, children and servants.

sources.reliability: Chalcedonian lawyer's history mixing church and state; uses Zosimus, Procopius, Priscus, Malalas and Eustathius.
sources.summary: Lawyer at Antioch, adviser to Patriarch Gregory.

sources.name: Chronicle of Pseudo-Zachariah Rhetor

works.note: Includes a Syriac version of Zachariah of Mytilene's church history (451-491), Anastasius' Persian war, the Huns and the Caucasus, and a description of Rome.

sources.reliability: Miaphysite Syriac compilation; valuable for eastern frontier events and steppe peoples.
sources.summary: Anonymous Amidene monk, 569.

sources.name: Menander Protector

works.books: Large fragments in the Excerpta de legationibus
works.note: The Fifty Years' Peace of 561/562 with its terms quoted; embassies of Zemarchus to the Turks (569) and to the Avars.

sources.reliability: Excellent diplomatic source with treaty texts and envoy reports; continues Agathias.
sources.summary: Imperial guardsman under Maurice.

sources.name: John of Ephesus

works.note: Justin II, Tiberius, Maurice; Slav invasion of 581-584; persecution of Miaphysites. Parts I-II survive partially through the Chronicle of Zuqnin (incl. the plague of 542).

sources.reliability: Miaphysite bishop with court access; vivid, partisan, written partly in prison.
sources.summary: Missionary bishop who converted thousands of pagans in Asia Minor for Justinian.

sources.name: Gregory of Tours

works.note: Books 1-2 to Clovis; 5-10 detailed contemporary history of 575-591.

sources.reliability: The main source for Merovingian Gaul; Catholic and episcopal viewpoint, story-telling over analysis; his Clovis narrative is shaped by hagiographic models.
sources.summary: Bishop of Tours from 573, of Gallo-Roman senatorial family.

sources.name: Strategikon of Maurice

works.note: Cavalry tactics, camp organization, how to fight Persians, Avars and Turks, Slavs and Franks.

sources.reliability: Practical late 6th-century field manual; key evidence for the transition of the Roman army toward cavalry archers and Avar-style equipment (stirrups).
sources.summary: Attributed to Maurice or a general of his court.

sources.name: Theophylact Simocatta

works.note: Maurice's reign: Balkan wars against Avars and Slavs, Persian war and the restoration of Khosrow II (591), the mutiny and murder of 602; with a retrospective from 572.

sources.reliability: Last classicizing historian; ornate style, chronological confusion in the Balkan narrative, but well-informed through official sources.
sources.summary: Egyptian, secretary under Heraclius; wrote c. 630.

sources.name: Isidore of Seville

works.note: Two recensions (619, 624); the latter praises Suintila's expulsion of the Byzantines.

sources.reliability: Primary source for the Visigothic kingdom to 624; Hispano-Gothic patriotism.
sources.summary: Bishop of Seville from c. 600.

sources.name: George of Pisidia

works.note: Expeditio Persica (622), Bellum Avaricum (siege of 626), Heraclias (628).

sources.reliability: Court poet and deacon at Hagia Sophia; contemporary witness to Heraclius' campaigns and the siege of 626, used by Theophanes.
sources.summary: Deacon and chartophylax of Hagia Sophia.

sources.name: Chronicon Paschale

works.note: Easter-chronicle from Adam to 628 (the text breaks off); with lacunae in the 6th century. Eyewitness record of the Avar-Persian siege of Constantinople (626) and the text of Heraclius' victory dispatch of 628.

sources.reliability: Based on consular lists and Malalas for earlier periods; primary for 600-628.
sources.summary: Anonymous Constantinopolitan cleric, c. 630.

sources.name: Sebeos

works.note: Armenia between Rome and Persia from the revolt of 572, Khosrow II's war, Heraclius' campaigns, the rise of Islam and the earliest non-Muslim account of Muhammad.

sources.reliability: Near-contemporary and well-informed, written c. 660; attribution to Bishop Sebeos is uncertain.
sources.summary: Armenian churchman.

sources.name: Chronicle of Fredegar

works.note: Own material for 584-642; earlier books abridge Jerome, Hydatius and Gregory; notes Heraclius and the Arabs, the Slav ruler Samo.

sources.reliability: Merovingian chronicle in barbarous Latin; key for 7th-century Francia and western perceptions of Byzantium.
sources.summary: Anonymous Burgundian compiler(s); 'Fredegar' is a 16th-century attribution.

sources.name: John of Nikiu

works.note: World chronicle surviving only in an Ethiopic translation (1602); a lacuna removes most of 610-639; the end gives a near-contemporary account of the Arab conquest of Egypt (639-642).

sources.reliability: Garbled in transmission but the only substantial contemporary non-Muslim narrative of the conquest of Egypt.
sources.summary: Coptic bishop of Nikiu in the Delta, writing c. 690.

sources.name: Khuzistan Chronicle

works.note: Late Sasanian civil wars, Heraclius' campaign, the Arab conquest of Iraq and Khuzistan.

sources.reliability: East Syrian Christian chronicle written c. 660; contemporary witness for the fall of the Sasanians.
sources.summary: Anonymous, Church of the East.

sources.name: Paul the Deacon

works.note: Lombard origins, Alboin's invasion of 568, the dukes, Agilulf and Theodelinda, Rothari; uses the lost history of Secundus of Trent.

sources.reliability: Late (written c. 790) but the essential narrative for Lombard Italy; folk traditions mixed with chronicles.
sources.summary: Lombard monk at Monte Cassino and Charlemagne's court.

sources.name: Theophanes the Confessor

works.note: Annalistic year-by-year chronicle (Annus Mundi) from Diocletian to 813; for 602-641 it is the main Byzantine narrative of Phocas, Heraclius' Persian war (from George of Pisidia and dispatches) and the Arab conquests (from an eastern Greek source shared with Syriac chronicles).

sources.reliability: Late, and its year-dates are often off by one or more years, but indispensable for the 7th century; compiled partly from George Syncellus' materials.
sources.summary: Monk and abbot; exiled for opposing Iconoclasm.

sources.name: al-Tabari
sources.latin: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari

works.t: History of the Prophets and Kings (Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk), Sasanian section
works.note: Ardashir to Yazdegerd III, from Arabic translations of the Middle Persian Khwaday-namag ('Book of Lords'); then the conquests year by year from 632.

sources.reliability: Preserves the late Sasanian court tradition, idealizing (Khosrow I as just king) and legendary in places (Bahram Gur), but with genuine administrative detail; Nöldeke's annotated translation (1879) remains fundamental.
sources.summary: Persian-born scholar in Baghdad.

sources.name: Zonaras

works.note: From creation to 1118. For Rome: books 7-9 from Dio's lost books 1-21 (to 146 BC), then Plutarch for 146-44 BC; books 10-11 from Dio to Severus Alexander; book 12 the 3rd century from lost sources (perhaps Peter the Patrician and the 'Leoquelle'); then Eusebius, Socrates, Theophanes.

sources.reliability: A careful 12th-century epitomator; our main witness for Dio's lost early books and for parts of the 3rd-century crisis.
sources.summary: Byzantine official (droungarios tes viglas) who became a monk.
